The violin is a wooden chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322-71, the smallest and highest-pitched member of the violin family. It usually has a hollow wooden body, four strings, occasionally five, mostly tuned in perfect fifths; it is played mainly with the bow, but the strings can also be plucked, and in special cases struck with the wood of the bow. It is used in Western classical chamber music, orchestras and solo playing, and is also found in country, bluegrass and jazz; an electric violin has a solid body and a piezoelectric pickup and is connected to an amplifier and speakers, for rock and jazz fusion, and has entered non-Western music such as that of India and Iran.
小提琴音色明亮透徹，具有溫潤而富有歌唱性的質感，極富表現力。其音域寬廣，跨越接近: The violin's tone is bright and clear, warm and singing, and highly expressive. Its range is wide, spanning nearly four octaves: the top is sharp and piercing, the middle warm and full, the bottom deep and heavy, so it can show many layers of feeling. The strings and the body vibrating together give the violin its own resonance, which lends the tone a soft sheen. Where the viola is calm and inward, the violin carries further; beside the lean, deep power of the cello, the violin sounds agile and fine. Its tone can be as gentle as a voice or as high as an eagle's cry, and changes of bowing and of stopping let it range from the lightest detail to full ardour. It is the most dramatically expressive instrument in the orchestra.
